intro: Four notes — E, C, E♭ and C♯ — supply twenty variations and a coda. Copland’s orchestration of his 1930 piano work gives the opening’s ringing C♯ to a soft horn and lets a flute-and-oboe duet emerge from the keyboard’s hard-edged lines.

cues.title: Four notes and an after-ring
cues.text: E, C, E♭, C♯: four notes generate the whole piece. In the piano original, a silently held key lets C♯ ring after the other notes are struck. Here a horn holds that note softly after a clang of brass and percussion.
cues.evidence: Kyle Gann’s American Symphony Orchestra note identifies the four-note idea and explains how the horn takes over the piano’s sympathetic resonance. https://americansymphony.org/concert-notes/orchestral-variantions-1957/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The theme becomes quieter
cues.text: Copland reverses the usual order of a variation set: the theme arrives forcefully, and its first variation is more subdued. The same four notes can make a hard chord or a line that threads between instruments.
cues.evidence: Barbara Heninger’s Redwood Symphony note explains the reversal between the forceful theme and the subdued first variation; Sidney Finkelstein’s Vanguard sleeve note discusses the lyricism disclosed by the orchestration. https://redwoodsymphony.org/piece/orchestral-variations/
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Twenty-seven years later
cues.text: Copland writes the piano piece in 1930 and returns to it in 1957 for a Louisville Orchestra commission. Robert Whitney conducts the orchestral première in Louisville on 5 March 1957.
cues.evidence: The Aaron Copland Fund’s work catalogue documents the piano original, the orchestration, the commission and the première. https://www.aaroncopland.com/works/orchestral-variations/

cues.title: Flute and oboe
cues.text: A quiet woodwind passage opens the middle of the piece. Flute and oboe share the eleventh variation; the four-note idea can now stretch into a duet before the quicker variations take hold.
cues.evidence: Kyle Gann identifies the flute-and-oboe duet in Variation XI and the build beginning in Variation XII; Heninger describes the slow, quiet woodwind centre. https://americansymphony.org/concert-notes/orchestral-variantions-1957/ ; https://redwoodsymphony.org/piece/orchestral-variations/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The beat slips
cues.text: The later variations send quick notes darting between instruments. One rhythm pushes against another, the beat dropping away and catching up again. The opening four notes remain underneath the changes of pace.
cues.evidence: Heninger describes the quick figures and rhythmic changes of Variations XII–XIX. Finkelstein’s Vanguard sleeve note describes the interplay of rhythms, especially from Variation XV onwards. https://redwoodsymphony.org/piece/orchestral-variations/ ; https://archive.org/download/lp_three-jewish-poems-for-orchestra-fanfare_ernest-bloch-aaron-copland-the-hartford-sy/lp_three-jewish-poems-for-orchestra-fanfare_ernest-bloch-aaron-copland-the-hartford-sy_djvu.txt
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bongos beside tubular bells
cues.text: The orchestral score adds bongos, conga drum and cowbell to a percussion group that also includes tubular bells, glockenspiel and xylophone. Copland gives the old piano piece a much larger cupboard of instruments.
cues.evidence: The Aaron Copland Fund’s catalogue lists the percussion instruments in the 1957 orchestral version. https://www.aaroncopland.com/works/orchestral-variations/

cues.title: Four notes fill the orchestra
cues.text: The coda broadens the short exchanges into heavy orchestral chords. Brass and percussion recover the force of the opening, now at the end of twenty variations made from the same four notes.
cues.evidence: Heninger describes the last variations building towards a full-orchestra coda; the Vanguard sleeve identifies the complete sequence as twenty variations and coda. https://redwoodsymphony.org/piece/orchestral-variations/ ; https://archive.org/download/lp_three-jewish-poems-for-orchestra-fanfare_ernest-bloch-aaron-copland-the-hartford-sy/lp_three-jewish-poems-for-orchestra-fanfare_ernest-bloch-aaron-copland-the-hartford-sy_djvu.txt
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: A Brooklyn modernist gave America its open fifths, its cowboy dances and a fanfare slow enough to let the brass ring.
facts: Rubin Goldmark in New York; Nadia Boulanger in Fontainebleau and Paris, 1921–24
Composer, pianist, conductor and writer; taught at Tanglewood, 1940–65

composer.background:
The Copland family lived above and beside their department store on Washington Avenue in Brooklyn. Aaron, born on 14 November 1900, was the youngest of Sarah and Harris Copland’s five children. His parents were Russian-born Jewish immigrants; everyone helped in the shop. His sister Laurine gave him his first piano lessons. When he wanted professional lessons, his parents let him find a teacher and agreed to pay. By 1917 he was crossing the Brooklyn Bridge to study harmony and counterpoint with Rubin Goldmark.

At Fontainebleau in 1921, a friend persuaded him to sit in on Nadia Boulanger’s harmony class. She became his composition teacher, and the planned year abroad stretched to three. In Paris he encountered Stravinsky’s music and heard the latest concert works. Boulanger took him to meet Serge Koussevitzky, who was about to take over the Boston Symphony Orchestra. The visit produced a commission: a symphony with Boulanger herself at the organ.
